title: Sicily
description: The Mediterranean's largest island: sun-soaked Nero d'Avola, volcanic Etna and historic Marsala.
L: Sicily is the largest island in the Mediterranean, at the toe of Italy, with about 98,000 hectares of vines, among Italy's largest wine regions. It has hills, plains, coasts and Mount Etna, Europe's highest active volcano, in the east. Smaller islands like Pantelleria and the Aeolian Islands also make wine.

The climate is Mediterranean: hot, dry summers, mild winters and plenty of sun. Constant winds and sea breezes keep vines healthy, so organic farming is common; Sicily has one of Italy's largest organic vineyard areas. Altitude, on Etna and inland hills, brings freshness. Drought is the main challenge.
Wind and sun keep vines healthy
Why is organic farming common in Sicily?
Wind and dry air keep vines healthy, needing fewer sprays.

For centuries, Sicily made bulk wine, often shipped north to blend, and Marsala, a fortified wine developed by English merchants from 1773. Since the 1990s, producers have focused on native grapes and quality. The Sicilia DOC, created in 2011, covers the whole island; Cerasuolo di Vittoria is its only DOCG.
Marsala was developed by English merchants.
Sicily is the Mediterranean's largest island
Its dry, windy climate suits organic farming
It moved from bulk wine to quality native grapes
Explain the role of international grapes

Nero d'Avola is Sicily's most planted red: dark, juicy, with black cherry, plum and fresh acidity. Nerello Mascalese, on Etna, gives pale, perfumed, firm wines; Nerello Cappuccio is its partner. Frappato, in the south-east, gives light, floral reds and blends with Nero d'Avola in Cerasuolo di Vittoria.

Catarratto is Sicily's most planted grape, used for everyday whites and Marsala. Grillo, a cross of Catarratto and Muscat of Alexandria, gives fresh, citrus whites and is a Marsala grape. Carricante, on Etna, gives taut, citrus, age-worthy whites. Zibibbo, Muscat of Alexandria, makes sweet Passito di Pantelleria.
Match each grape to its role.
Sicily's grapes are native and varied.
Look for Grillo from western Sicily. It's a fresh, citrus white that offers great value.
Which is Sicily's most planted grape?
Catarratto, a white grape, covers the most area.
Nero d'Avola, Nerello Mascalese and Frappato lead the reds
Catarratto, Grillo and Carricante lead the whites

Etna's vineyards climb its slopes from about 400 to over 1,000 m, mostly on the north, east and south sides. Altitude gives cool nights and late harvests into October. Soils are volcanic sand, ash and lava, poor and well-drained. Phylloxera can't survive easily, so many old vines are ungrafted bush vines, alberello, on terraces.

Etna's vineyards are divided into contrade, local districts often defined by different lava flows. Since 2011, 133 contrade can appear on labels, like Burgundy's crus. Etna DOC, one of Italy's first, from 1968, covers red, white, rosé and sparkling. Etna Rosso must be at least 80% Nerello Mascalese; Etna Bianco at least 60% Carricante.
Local districts often defined by lava flows
Each contrada has its own soil and character.

Etna's modern revival began around 2000, when producers like Frank Cornelissen, Andrea Franchetti and Marc de Grazia arrived, and local families like Benanti invested. Its reds, pale and perfumed, are often compared with Burgundy and Barolo. Its whites, from Carricante, are mineral and long-lived.
Etna's vineyards are steep and poor, not flat and fertile.
Etna's vineyards climb to over 1,000 m on volcanic soils
Its revival since 2000 made Nerello and Carricante famous
Reading Sicily and eating with it

Labels show Sicilia DOC, Etna DOC, Cerasuolo di Vittoria DOCG, or Terre Siciliane IGT. Marsala, in the west, is a fortified wine from Grillo, Catarratto and Inzolia; styles range from Fine, a year old, to Vergine, dry, aged at least five years, often in a solera. It's Sicily's historic wine.

Nero d'Avola suits pasta alla Norma, with aubergine and ricotta, grilled meat and pizza. Etna Rosso suits tuna, swordfish, mushrooms and lamb. Grillo and Carricante suit seafood, raw fish and caponata. Passito di Pantelleria suits cannoli, Sicily's ricotta pastries. Dry Marsala Vergine suits aged cheese.
Which wine is a classic with cannoli?
Sweet Zibibbo from Pantelleria suits ricotta pastries.
Marsala Vergine, dry and nutty, is very different from the cooking Marsala many people know. Try it as an aperitif with almonds.
Marsala Vergine is a dry style.
Yes, aged at least five years.
Labels show Sicilia DOC, Etna DOC or Terre Siciliane IGT
Marsala ranges from young Fine to dry Vergine
Pair Nero d'Avola with pasta alla Norma; Pantelleria with cannoli
Match each wine to its place.
Not true. Cerasuolo di Vittoria is its only DOCG.
Etna's local vineyard districts are called ____.
Contrade, often defined by lava flows.
Sicily is hot, dry and windy, with native grapes
Etna's volcanic slopes make its finest wines
Marsala and Pantelleria are its historic sweet wines
